title: Descriptive Statistics
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Statistics is the science of learning from data. Descriptive statistics summarize data; inferential statistics draw conclusions about populations from samples. Measures of center: mean (average, sensitive to outliers), median (middle, robust), mode (most frequent). Measures of spread: range, variance (average squared deviation), standard deviation (typical distance from mean). Percentiles and quartiles. The shape of data: symmetric, skewed, bimodal. Visualization: histograms, box plots, scatter plots reveal patterns numbers alone hide.

WORKED EXAMPLE: For data {2, 3, 3, 4, 100}, the mean is 22.4 (pulled up by the outlier 100), but the median is 3 (unaffected). This is why median income is reported instead of mean — a few billionaires distort the average. Choosing the right measure of center is the first act of honest statistics.

PRACTICE: 1) Find the mean, median, and mode of {5,7,7,9,12}. 2) Explain when median beats mean. 3) Calculate the range of a dataset.

title: Probability Foundations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Probability quantifies uncertainty from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Sample space (all outcomes), events (subsets). The addition rule (P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)) and multiplication rule for independent events (P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B)). Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Independence vs mutual exclusivity (different concepts). Combinations and permutations count possibilities. Expected value (probability-weighted average) drives rational decisions under uncertainty.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Rolling two dice, P(sum=7) = 6/36 = 1/6 (six ways: 1-6, 2-5, 3-4, 4-3, 5-2, 6-1 out of 36 outcomes). Seven is the most likely sum, which is why it's central in games of chance. Counting outcomes correctly — the sample space — is the foundation of all probability.

PRACTICE: 1) Find P(drawing a heart) from a deck. 2) Compute expected value of a $10 bet with 30% win chance for $50. 3) Explain independence vs mutual exclusivity.

title: Distributions
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A probability distribution describes how likely each outcome is. Discrete: binomial (n trials, success probability p — coin flips, defect rates), Poisson (rare events over time). Continuous: the normal distribution (bell curve) is central — defined by mean and standard deviation; the 68-95-99.7 rule (data within 1, 2, 3 SDs). The Central Limit Theorem: sample means are normally distributed regardless of the underlying distribution — the reason the normal curve is everywhere. Standardization (z-scores) compares across distributions. Uniform, exponential distributions model other phenomena.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Human heights are normally distributed. If mean = 170cm, SD = 10cm, then ~68% of people are 160-180cm, ~95% are 150-190cm (2 SDs). A z-score of +2 (190cm) means you're taller than ~97.5% of people. The normal distribution turns 'how unusual is this?' into a precise probability — the workhorse of statistics.

title: Sampling & Estimation
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: We rarely measure whole populations, so we sample. A good sample is random and representative — bias (systematic error) is the enemy (selection bias, response bias, survivorship bias). Sample statistics estimate population parameters. The standard error measures sampling variability (shrinks with larger samples: SE = σ/√n). Confidence intervals give a range likely to contain the true parameter (a 95% CI means: if we repeated sampling many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the truth — NOT '95% chance the truth is in this one'). Larger samples give more precise estimates.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A poll of 1,000 people finds 52% support with a ±3% margin of error (95% CI: 49-55%). Because the interval includes 50%, the race is a statistical tie — the 52% could be sampling noise. Misreading this (declaring a 2-point 'lead') is the most common statistical error in media. The margin of error is not decoration; it defines what the data can and cannot claim.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain why random sampling matters. 2) Describe what a 95% confidence interval means correctly. 3) Explain how sample size affects the margin of error.

title: Hypothesis Testing
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Hypothesis testing decides whether data provides evidence for a claim. The null hypothesis (H₀: no effect) vs alternative (H₁: an effect). A p-value is the probability of seeing data this extreme IF the null were true — small p (<0.05 conventionally) suggests the null is unlikely. Critically, p-value is NOT the probability the null is true, and statistical significance ≠ practical importance. Type I error (false positive, rejecting a true null) vs Type II (false negative). Statistical power. The replication crisis stems from p-hacking and misunderstanding these tools.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A drug trial gets p = 0.03. This means: if the drug did nothing, there's a 3% chance of seeing results this strong by luck. It does NOT mean '97% chance the drug works.' With thousands of trials, some will hit p<0.05 by pure chance (why replication matters). Understanding what a p-value actually says — and doesn't — separates real evidence from statistical illusion.

PRACTICE: 1) State what a p-value actually means. 2) Distinguish Type I from Type II error. 3) Explain why statistical significance isn't practical importance.

title: Regression & Correlation
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Correlation (r, from −1 to +1) measures linear association strength and direction — but correlation is NOT causation. Linear regression fits a line (y = mx + b) minimizing squared errors (least squares), predicting one variable from another. R² measures variance explained. Multiple regression uses several predictors. Residual analysis checks assumptions. Confounding variables and spurious correlations mislead. Regression to the mean (extreme values tend toward average) fools intuition constantly. Regression is the foundation of predictive modeling and much of data science.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A study finds a 0.8 correlation between coffee drinking and heart disease. Does coffee cause it? Maybe — or smokers drink more coffee (confounding: smoking causes both). Correlation of 0.8 is strong association, but establishing causation requires controlled experiments or careful confounding control. Mistaking correlation for causation is the single most consequential statistical error in science, business, and policy.

PRACTICE: 1) Interpret a correlation of −0.9. 2) Explain what R² measures. 3) Give an example of a confounding variable creating a spurious correlation.

title: Grandmaster — Bayesian & Advanced Methods
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Bayesian statistics treats probability as degree of belief, updated with evidence via Bayes' theorem: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. This contrasts with frequentist methods (probability as long-run frequency). Bayesian thinking is natural for updating beliefs and underlies modern machine learning. Advanced methods: ANOVA (comparing multiple groups), chi-square tests (categorical data), non-parametric tests (no distribution assumptions), time series analysis, and experimental design (randomization, control, blocking). Multiple comparisons require correction (Bonferroni) — testing many hypotheses guarantees false positives.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A rare disease affects 1 in 1,000. A test is 99% accurate. You test positive. Bayesian updating: prior (0.001) × likelihood, weighed against the ~1% false-positive rate across 999 healthy people, gives a posterior of only ~9% — not 99%. Bayes' theorem formally combines the base rate (prior) with the evidence (test), producing the correct answer that pure intuition gets catastrophically wrong.

PRACTICE: 1) State Bayes' theorem in words (posterior ∝ likelihood × prior). 2) Explain the difference between Bayesian and frequentist views. 3) Explain why multiple comparisons require correction.

title: King Level — Statistics as the Science of Evidence
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, statistics is the discipline of reasoning correctly under uncertainty — the immune system against being fooled by randomness, bias, and our own pattern-seeking minds. It underlies all empirical science, evidence-based medicine, data-driven business, and machine learning. The deepest lessons: distinguish signal from noise, correlation from causation, and significance from importance; respect uncertainty rather than false precision; and recognize that data can be tortured to confess anything (p-hacking, cherry-picking, misleading visualizations). The King-level truth: statistics is less about computation than about intellectual honesty — the willingness to quantify uncertainty, follow evidence even when unwelcome, and resist the powerful human urge to see patterns in noise. In a world drowning in data and claims, statistical literacy is a fundamental defense against manipulation and self-deception.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A company runs 20 A/B tests; one shows a 'significant' 5% lift (p<0.05). They roll it out — and it fails. Why? With 20 tests at the 5% threshold, one false positive is expected by pure chance. The 'winner' was noise. The statistically literate leader knew this (multiple comparisons) and demanded replication before acting. This single habit — demanding that findings replicate — separates data-driven decisions from data-fooled ones.

PRACTICE: 1) Explain how running many tests produces false positives. 2) Describe three ways data can mislead. 3) Reflect on why statistics is fundamentally about intellectual honesty.
